Collar
KOL-ar
n. (the neck-band of a coat; in Job, the disease that binds like one)
From Latin collare, a band for the neck, from collum, neck. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Job's lament, where his disease has changed his garment and binds him about as the collar of his coat.

Biblical Definition

By the great force of my disease is my garment changed: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat. Job is describing what the sickness has done to his own skin, and he reaches for a piece of clothing to say it: the thing is not upon him, it is around him, close and constricting at the throat, like the neck of a garment that no longer fits. Two chapters earlier he had used clothing for the opposite condition: I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem. The same man in the same book is clothed twice, once in the respect of the city gate and once in the disease that has replaced it. Between the two lies everything the book is about. He does not deny the change, minimise it, or make peace with it prematurely: he hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes; my harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep. Scripture gives a suffering man this vocabulary on purpose. Lament is not unbelief, and Job is vindicated at the end of the book against the friends who wanted his complaints tidied away.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): something worn round the neck, as a ring of metal or the part of a garment which surrounds the neck; in Scripture, the figure Job uses for his binding disease.

expand to see more

COLLAR, n. Something worn round the neck, as a ring of metal, or a chain.

COLLAR, n. The part of a garment which surrounds the neck.

DISEASE, n. In a general sense, pain, uneasiness, distress; any deviation from health.

LAMENT, v.i. To mourn; to grieve; to weep or wail; to express sorrow.

AFFLICTION, n. The cause of continued pain of body or mind, as sickness, losses, calamity, adversity.

Key Scripture

Job 30:18 — "By the great force of my disease is my garment changed: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat."

Job 29:14 — "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem."

Job 30:19 — "He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes."

Job 30:31 — "My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep."

Modern Corruption

Suffering is handled either with therapeutic vocabulary that treats it as a wound to be processed or with a false piety that forbids complaint; Job's language is given in Scripture as a sanctioned register for grief before God.

expand to see more

A great deal of modern counsel about affliction has borrowed a vocabulary that Scripture does not use and abandoned the one it does. The Bible's categories for Job's condition are suffering, affliction, the hand of God, the breaking of a man under a curse he did not personally earn, and the language it gives him is blunt and physical — the collar of his coat, the mire, dust and ashes, the harp turned to mourning. That vocabulary is more honest than the clinical one and far more honest than the pious one that hurries a sufferer past the lament to the application.

The other corruption is the friends' and it is the one God rebukes by name. They could not tolerate an unexplained affliction and so they explained it, and every explanation was an accusation. At the end the LORD said to Eliphaz, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. The man who complained bitterly and would not curse God is the one commended. The dictionary takes that as its rule for the ministry of comfort: sit seven days, speak little, and never explain what God has not explained.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew peh (H6310), a mouth or opening, and so the neck-hole of a garment; kuttoneth (H3801), a coat or tunic; chaphas (H2664), to be changed or disguised.

expand to see more

Hebrew peh (H6310) — a mouth, an opening; the collar or neck-opening of the coat.

Hebrew kuttoneth (H3801) — a tunic, a coat; the same word as Joseph's coat of many colours.

Hebrew chaphas (H2664) — to disguise, to change; my garment is changed.

Hebrew 'azar (H247) — to gird, to bind about; it bindeth me about.

Hebrew 'ebel (H60) — mourning; my harp also is turned to mourning.

Usage

"“it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat” — the single occurrence."

"“I put on righteousness, and it clothed me” — the garment he had worn before."

"“My harp also is turned to mourning” — lament as sanctioned speech."
